newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia wants apology from Lee over remarks.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia wants apology from Lee over remarks.

text.p: Malaysia asked Singapore's Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew on Wednesday to apologise and retract a statement criticising a Malaysian state as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
"If the Senior Minister really values our goodwill, he should retract his statement and tender an apology," Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said in a statement.
Abdullah said he was "extremely shocked at the sentiments and derogatory statement made by Mr Lee Kuan Yew, a Senior Minister of the Singapore government, on Johor."
Abdullah issued the statement after meeting Singapore's deputy high commissioner (ambassador) Vanu Gopala Menon, who was summoned to his office.

"I do not believe that such (a) callous statement could help to inspire confidence in the efforts to maintain good and friendly relations between Malaysia and Singapore...," Abdullah said in unusually harsh remarks from the foreign ministry.
"Such (a) statement could only convey hostility and an utter lack of concern and sensitivity for maintaining goodwill and friendship between Malaysia and Singapore," he said.
In a court affidavit filed in a Singapore court on January 27, Lee described Malaysia's Johor state, just across a causeway from Singapore, as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Lee's affidavit was filed in one of 13 libel lawsuits brought against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong after elections in January.
Other Malaysian politicians were also livid.

The chairman of the youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, said Lee's remarks were disrespectful, the national Bernama news agency reported.
"In fact, UMNO Youth regards his charges as nonsensical and illogical," Ahmad Zahid was quoted as saying in a statement.
Malaysia's opposition Democratic Action Party (DAP) said Lee should withdraw his statement.
"All Malaysians are angry at the insulting remarks and slur...," the party said in a statement.
Lee's affidavit came to light when a lawyer for opposition politican Tang released a transcript of it on Tuesday.

During Singapore's election campaign in January, government officials accused Tang, a prominent lawyer and advocate of Chinese culture, of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who threatened Singapore's racial harmony.
Tang called them "liars", prompting the lawsuits.
Tang fled to Johor soon after the polls, which the governing People's Action Party comfortably won, saying he had received death threats.

Malaysia and Singapore engaged in acrimonious exchanges last year when Lee raised the possibility of eventual reunification with Malaysia. But he said Kuala Lumpur must first end a policy of special rights for indigenous races and pursue meritocracy.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said then that Singapore was using his country as a "bogeyman" to scare voters ahead of the January polls.
Singapore broke away from the Malaysian Federation in 1965, in part over disagreement about the pro-Malay policy.
